research_scientist.headline: PhD just finished, first postdoc
research_scientist.why: A research CV is not a resume with a publication list bolted on. Publications, funding and talks are the currency and they are formatted so a panel can check them: author position marked, the preprint labelled as a preprint rather than dressed up as a paper, and every award given with its funder and period. Employment takes up less space than the sections underneath it, which is correct here and nowhere else. A real one would also carry an ORCID iD beside the contact line.

research_scientist.headline: Six years, industry research and patents
research_scientist.why: The industry version of a research CV, and the differences are the whole lesson. Publications survive but are cut to a selected list with the total stated; what leads instead is the thing an academic CV never has to show, which is what reached a product. Patents get their own block with the inventor position given, because in industrial research they are read the way papers are read in academia.

research_scientist.headline: Fifteen years, leads a research group
research_scientist.why: By this point the publication list is explicitly selected and the funding block has become the headline: funder, role, amount, period, in that order, because a panel reads it before anything else. What a senior research CV adds that an academic one at any earlier stage does not is a management dimension - the size of the group, the budget behind it and where its people went afterwards.
